Line 10 of Code Listing 22.2 includes the first instance in this book of the incre-

it follows by 1. So, if i , then the i; statement would set the value of i to .
There is also a decrement operator (). The decrement operator decreases the
value of the variable by 1.
You can place increment and decrement operators either before or after the
variable name, and doing so causes the statement to be treated differently (i.e.,
i and i act slightly differently). The difference is in whether the initial value
is returned (i) or whether the incremented value is returned (i). Here's an
example to clarify.
7 void Start() {
8 int i = 1;
9 print( i ); // Output: 1
10 print( i++ ); // Output: 1
11 print( i ); // Output: 2
12 print( ++i ); // Output: 3
13 }
As you can see, line 9 prints the current value of i, which is 1. Then, on line 10,
you can think of the post-increment operator i as first returning the current
value of i, which is printed (resulting in the 1), and then incrementing the i, set-
ting its value to 2.
Line 11 prints the current value of i, which is 2. Then, on line 12, the pre-increment
operator i first increments the value of i from 2 to 3 and then returns it to the
print function, which prints a 3.

In both the Zhile and doڕZhile examples, we needed to declare and define a variable

of these actions in a single line.

The for loop in this example sends the same output to the Console pane as was sent by
the "more useful" Zhile loop (in Code Listing 22.2), yet it does so in fewer lines of code.
The structure of a for loop requires an initialization clause, a condition clause, and an
iteration clause to be valid. In the above example, the three clauses are as follows:
Initialization clause: for ( int i ; i<3; i++ ) {
Condition clause: for ( int i=0; i; i++ ) {
Iteration clause: for ( int i=0; i<3; i ) {
The initialization clause ( int i ; ) is executed before the for loop begins.
It declares and defines a variable that is scoped locally to the for loop. This means
that the int i in the initialization clause will cease to exist when the for loop is
complete. For more information on variable scoping, see the "Variable Scope" section
of Appendix B, "Useful Concepts."
The condition clause ( i ) is checked before every iteration of the for loop, includ-
ing the first iteration (just as the condition clause is checked before the first iteration of a
Zhile loop). If the condition clause is true, the code between the braces of the for loop
is executed.
The iteration clause ( i ) is executed after each iteration of the code between the
braces of the for loop has completed (i.e., after each time that the lines between the
braces { } of the for loop execute—in this case, the single line print( /oop   i ); —
the i is executed).
After the iteration clause executes, the condition clause is checked again, and if the
condition clause is still true, the code between the braces is executed again, and the
iteration clause is executed again. This continues until the condition clause evaluates to
false, at which point the for loop ends.
Because for loops mandate that each of these three clauses be included and that they
all be on the same line, it is easier to avoid writing infinite loops when working with for
loops.

MODULO OPERATOR
Line 9 of Code Listing 22.10 for the continue jump statement is the first instance
in this book of the modulo operator ( ). Modulo (or more commonly, "mod")
returns the remainder of dividing one number by another. For example, 1   
would return a value of 2 because the remainder of 12/5 is 2 (5 goes into 12 two
times (5 × 2 = 10), leaving a remainder of 2).
Mod can also be used with floats, so 1.f   1f would return .f, because 1
goes into 12 twelve times, leaving 0.6 as the remainder.
Similarly, 1.f   .f would return .1f, because 0.5 goes into 12.6 twenty-
five times (0.5 × 25 = 12.5), leaving a remainder of 0.1.
However, because of the inaccuracy of float math, 1.f   .f could possibly
return .1f, which is not equal to .1f. If you are dealing with floats
and modulo, I highly recommend using approximate methods of comparing the
results. See the "Approximate Float Comparison" sidebar in Chapter 21, "Boolean
Operations and Conditionals," for more information.
Summary
Understanding loops is one of the key elements of becoming a good programmer.
However, it's fine if not all of this makes perfect sense now. After you start using loops
in the development of some actual game prototypes (like in Part III of this book!), it
will become more clear to you. Just make sure that you are actually typing each code
example into Unity and running it to help with your understanding of the material.
Also remember that in my coding, I commonly use for and foreach but rarely or never
use Zhile and doڕZhile because of the increased likelihood of Zhile and doڕZhile caus-
ing an infinite loop.
In the next chapter, you will learn about arrays and Lists, two forms of ordered
collections of similar items, and you will see how loops are used to iterate over these
collections. You will also learn about Dictionaries, a non-ordered collection, and some
other collections.

C# Collections
A collection is a group of objects that are referenced by a single variable. In regular life,
collections would be things like a group of people, a pride of lions, a parliament of
rooks, or a murder of crows. Just like these animal grouping terms, the collections we'll
use in C# can only hold a single type of data

Apart from the array, every other type of collection you see in this chapter is part

Choosing Whether to Use
an Array or List
Arrays and Lists are very similar, so people are often unsure which one to use in any
given situation. The primary differences between the array and List collection types are
as follows:
■ List has flexible length, whereas array length is more difficult to change.
■ Array allows multidimensional indices.
■ Array allows empty elements in the middle of the collection.

Some functions are called with empty parentheses following them (e.g., Print8pdates()
